answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Hawthorne. The exact line is spoken by the character Donatello in Hawthorne’s novel The Marble Faun (1860) — and Hawthorne’s own narrator immediately calls the remark “trite,” a wink the inspirational-poster versions always drop.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Marble Faun; or, The Romance of Monte Beni
Donatello, to the sculptor Kenyon, at the tower of Monte Beni

source.excerpt:
“I may have known such a life, when I was younger,” answered Donatello. “I am not a boy now. Time flies over us, but leaves its shadow behind.”

The sculptor could not but smile at the triteness of the remark, which, nevertheless, had a kind of originality as coming from Donatello.
trail: Search engines, Goodreads and Britannica all credit the line to Hawthorne — and here that credit holds up, per Britannica’s Hawthorne quotes.
The exact sentence is in The Marble Faun (1860), spoken by Donatello, confirmed in the Eldritch Press edition of the chapter.
The narrator immediately undercuts it: the sculptor smiles “at the triteness of the remark” — verifiable in the Gutenberg full text.
Not listed on Wikiquote’s Hawthorne page, and no Quote Investigator entry exists — so this page rests on the primary source itself.
source.excerptNote: Hawthorne gives the line to the simple, sorrow-changed Donatello — and has the narrator flag it as “trite” even as it lands. The aphorism is real Hawthorne; the earnest inspirational framing is not how the book treats it.

author.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
author.heading: About Nathaniel Hawthorne
author.bio: Nathaniel Hawthorne was a central figure of the American Romance tradition, author of The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). The Marble Faun (1860), written after years in Italy, was his last completed novel; in it the man-child Donatello is transformed by guilt and sorrow — the context in which this line about time’s lingering shadow is spoken.

misattribution.heading: A rare genuine one — with a catch
misattribution.intro: Hawthorne’s name is a notorious magnet for feel-good quotes he never wrote. This one, unusually, is his. The distortion here isn’t the author — it’s the tone.

items.why: The words are really Hawthorne’s, from The Marble Faun (1860). What’s usually lost is that he puts them in the mouth of the simple Donatello and has the narrator call the remark “trite” — see the chapter text.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: genuinely Nathaniel Hawthorne, The Marble Faun (1860) — verified word-for-word against the primary text.

context.heading: The scene behind the line
lead: In the novel, Kenyon imagines Donatello living an idyllic, Arcadian life of figs and sunlit grapes. Donatello — changed by a crime and its guilt — answers gravely that boyhood is behind him: “Time flies over us, but leaves its shadow behind.”

The line works precisely because of who says it. Hawthorne frames it as a homely truth a simple soul has “thought out from his own experience,” and the narrator’s smile at its “triteness” is part of the point. Stripped onto a poster, it reads as polished wisdom; in the book it’s tender, ironic, and a little sad.
context.pull: “I am not a boy now. Time flies over us, but leaves its shadow behind.”
